source.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
source.authors: Gouki Minegishi; Hiroki Furuta; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo

page_placements.theme: Whether one latent captures a concept depends on width (and layer); multi-latent composites recover it

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates SAE semantic performance on polysemous words, including across dictionary expansion ratios, but does not measure whether larger dictionaries split a coarse feature into related features that partition its inputs.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern polysemy metrics, not feature matching, input-set partitioning, or geometric proximity between features. The paper’s prompt for GPT-4 is an example evaluation prompt, not an instruction to an AI reading or reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates whether the max-activated SAE latent differs between contexts of polysemous words (PS-Eval on WiC) across expand ratios, activation functions, layers and components. It never matches latents across dictionary sizes, checks whether finer latents cover a coarse latent's inputs or lie near its direction, or examines families, absorption or decomposition. Its Bricken et al. citation on fine-grained features is motivation, not a test. None of V1–V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct, with one addition. The authors conclude that larger latent dimensions improve PS-Eval up to saturation, and that MSE–L0-optimised activation functions (TopK, JumpReLU) do not improve semantic extraction; ReLU ranks highest. They also report that deeper layers and attention outputs give higher specificity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains SAEs and evaluates maximum-activation features on WiC-derived polysemy metrics; it does not use a feature-matching or geometric splitting analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported polysemy metrics vary with expand ratio, layer, activation function, and training domain; the paper also reports differences across base models.

fits_no_version.finding: PS-Eval accuracy on GPT-2 small rises with expand ratio. Layer 4 saturates near ratio 64 (0.6669 at 64, 0.6576 at 128); layer 6 rises through 128 (0.6686).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger SAE dictionaries more often assign different max-activated latents to different word senses, up to a saturation point; this is sense separation, not tested splitting.

fits_no_version.finding: Open SAEs score near chance on accuracy for Pythia 70M (0.51) and Gemma2-2B (0.52), versus 0.66 for GPT-2 small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sense-level separation by open SAEs varies across base models and is not better for larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: ReLU SAEs get higher PS-Eval F1 than JumpReLU or TopK at both layer 4 (0.7623) and layer 6 (0.7509).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation functions that improve the MSE–L0 trade-off do not improve sense-level separation.

record.problems: The paper’s stated limitation is that maximum activation may reflect an unrelated aspect rather than the target word meaning, and the authors say this may make evaluation ambiguous. Most reported results concern GPT-2 small; open SAE results cover three models. The exact expansion-ratio accuracy table gives no uncertainty estimates, though the paper reports error bars across 3 seeds for an activation-function figure.
record.rows_left_out: Left out figure-only results for other PS-Eval metrics across expansion ratios, layers, and Transformer components, as well as qualitative logit-lens examples and MSE/L0 results: they do not measure the splitting behavior in the claim. Exact tabulated expansion-ratio accuracies, open-SAE metrics, and activation-function F1 values are included above.

untested.parts: All: no cross-size feature matching, no input-coverage analysis, no decoder-direction proximity.
All: open SAEs on GPT-2 small, Pythia 70M and Gemma2-2B get PS-Eval scores only, with no splitting analysis.
All: no feature families, nesting or hierarchy.
All: no parent/child latent firing analysis.
All: no decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents, and no count of novel latents.
All: activation-function comparisons (ReLU/TopK/JumpReLU) report PS-Eval only, not splitting.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6 / no-version classification is confirmed. No rows bear on any version, so no verdicts are given. The expand-ratio result concerns whether one max-activated latent differs per word sense. That is related to finer-grained features but does not measure replacement, input coverage or direction proximity. Appendix K open-SAE results come from a single SAE per base model.

versions.untested_parts: Whether coarse features are replaced by finer features, whether those features cover the same inputs, and whether their directions are nearby.
Whether the splitting pattern holds in large models or open SAE releases.
Whether feature families are nested, geometrically close, or mirror a hierarchy of concepts.
Whether parent and child latents overlap in firing, or whether size or sparsity changes fix that pattern.
Whether larger latents decompose into smaller-latent combinations or add novel latents.
Whether the splitting pattern is caused by the SAE objective, or whether Matryoshka SAEs change or reduce splitting.

relation.reason: Mentions only that larger dictionaries may learn finer-grained features (citing Bricken et al.) and measures expand-ratio effects on its own polysemy metric. It does not test splitting or use it as a tool.

tranche.reason: PS-Eval tests whether the max-activated SAE latent differs across meanings of a polysemous word. It never matches latents across dictionary sizes or checks coverage/direction, so it is a related but different construct.

source_check.notes: Table 10/11 text layout interleaves Layer 4/Layer 6 values per column; the pair reading is confirmed by Figure 3's 0.59-0.67 axis for layer 4. Open SAEs in Table 7 sit at different layers (Gemma2-2B at layer 20) and not at expand ratio 32.
